newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa considers mineral rights tax.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa considers mineral rights tax.

text.p: The South African government is considering a mineral rights tax to encourage the transfer or sale of unused mineral rights to the state when not being used, Minerals and Energy Minister Penuell Maduna said on Wednesday.

Opening the debate on his 1997/98 budget, South Africa's first black mines minister said this was part of a new programme to ensure mineral rights were more widely held, especially by blacks who had been excluded from owning mines by apartheid.

Maduna, appointed last year, took over from the National Party's Pik Botha when the NP left the government of national 5nity and has been involved in a widescale restructuring of his department and policies for the last 10 months.
He said black South Africans had been dispossessed of their mining rights since 1872 and had been reduced to being only a source of cheap labour in mines.
"The injustice of our past which is eminent within the current configuration ought to be dealt with," Maduna said.

The current system of mineral rights being held by both the state and the private sector was a deterrent to potential foreign investors as well as new black entrants, while the private ownership of mineral rights was an exception rather than a rule in other countries, he said.
"People with a vested interest in the dual system argue that we must be careful lest any increased availability of mineral rights leads to overproduction and lower prices," Maduna said.
"It is also true that security of tenure where there is geological potential is one of the most important considerations to investors."

But a World Bank study had found that countries that had attracted the most investment in exploration had shown that state ownership of mineral rights was not incompatible with security of tenure and title.
Maduna said he realised that changing the system would face constitutional as well as practical problems, but he believed that steps could still be taken to change the situation.

These included granting prospecting and mining rights over alienated state land, introducing a mineral rights tax, annual minimum work or investment requirements to discourage the holding of unprmductive mineral rights and properties. -- Parliamentary newsroom +27 21 403-2502
